A scientist may accurately state that the global mean temperature has increased x degrees but for laymen living in an area going through a record cold front that's might seem like a bizarre statement.

A 65 degree average would be the same thing as 4 months at 45 degrees and 8 months at 75. Massage those values in either direction and you'll get something pretty representative. And keep in mind that's the overall average so don't forget to compensate for night time.

VIrginia shows a clear trend upwards starting in the seventies. While some of that has to do with man-made climate change, I think the statewide average has also been skewed upwards due to the rapid urbanization and growth of the major metros. Anyone that lives in a city is aware of the heat amplification and retention effect known as an urban heat island, and given that over six million of Virginia's 8.5'million people occupy urban areas stretching long distances, I would think that has to at least contribute.

The cool thing is you could test your hypothesis out. Compare and contrast states that have experienced major increased urbanization with those that have remained mostly rural. The two states that came to mind for this for me were California and Montana. Interestingly enough California's average temperature has "only" increased by a bit over 2 degrees whereas Montana has increased a clear 3 degrees. One counter example in something with as much variance as climate isn't necessarily enough to entirely refute the hypothesis, but it's not looking good for it!
